sources.title: Internet Protocol
sources.claim: IPv4 headers carry source and destination addresses; the level shows only the fields needed for its model.

sources.title: Internet Control Message Protocol
sources.claim: ICMP Time Exceeded messages are used as background for the game's simplified traceroute reveal.

sources.title: Security Architecture for the Internet Protocol
sources.claim: The ordered first-match filter in this lesson is an explicitly simplified game policy, not a universal firewall configuration.

sources.title: Transmission Control Protocol
sources.claim: TCP provides a reliable, in-order byte-stream service with retransmission behavior.

sources.title: User Datagram Protocol
sources.claim: UDP is transaction-oriented and does not guarantee delivery or duplicate protection; applications may add recovery.

sources.title: Requirements for Internet Hosts - Communication Layers
sources.section: 3.3.1.1-3.3.1.2; updated by RFC 9293 for TCP requirements
sources.claim: A host distinguishes local destinations from remote ones and uses a configured gateway for off-link traffic.

sources.title: Classless Inter-domain Routing
sources.claim: A slash prefix denotes the significant leading bits used to represent an IPv4 network.

sources.title: Definition of the Differentiated Services Field
sources.section: 3; updated by RFC 3168, RFC 3260, and RFC 8436
sources.claim: Differentiated services use a header field to support service discrimination; the game's queue order is a local policy.

sources.title: Configuration Guidelines for DiffServ Service Classes
sources.section: 1.4.1 and 2.1-2.3; updated by RFC 5865 and RFC 8622
sources.claim: Service classes can use configured queuing behavior; these guidelines are informational rather than universal guarantees.

sources.title: TCP Congestion Control
sources.claim: TCP congestion control responds to congestion; the lesson's finite delay and loss traces are a game model.

sources.title: IETF Recommendations Regarding Active Queue Management
sources.claim: The document recommends active queue management; it does not imply a single queue or loss behavior in every network.

levels.title: Choose the route
levels.learningOutcome: Compare hop count and total latency to choose a lowest-latency path.
levels.briefing: Links show latency in milliseconds. Add the values along a route; fewer hops do not always mean less delay. The traceroute reveal shows one probe's hops, not a universal best path.

hints.method: Count the links, then add each route's displayed latency values. Compare totals, not just hop counts.
hints.solution: The short route is 2 hops and 80 ms. Both the upper and lower routes are 3 hops and 30 ms, so either is a correct minimum.

completion.required: Reach the destination using any available lowest-latency route.

checkpoints.title: Choose the route
checkpoints.briefing: Links show latency in milliseconds. Add the values along a route; fewer hops do not always mean less delay. The traceroute reveal shows one probe's hops, not a universal best path.

hints.method: Count the links, then add each route's displayed latency values. Compare totals, not just hop counts.
hints.solution: The short route is 2 hops and 80 ms. Both the upper and lower routes are 3 hops and 30 ms, so either is a correct minimum.

checkpoints.title: A faster express link
checkpoints.briefing: New measurements apply only to this checkpoint's next network segment. Recalculate every route: the shortest route can now be fastest.

hints.method: Add the new link values; do not reuse the previous checkpoint's answer.
hints.solution: The direct route totals 12 ms, upper 45 ms, and lower 55 ms. Choose the direct route.

checkpoints.title: Route around an outage
checkpoints.briefing: The direct route has a failed link. Compare only available routes using this checkpoint's new measurements.

hints.method: Reject any route with a failed link before comparing latency.
hints.solution: The upper route is available and totals 9 ms; lower totals 24 ms. Direct is unavailable. Choose upper.

ghostQuestions.prompt: Route A has two 40 ms links. Route B has three 10 ms links. Both are available. Which has lower total latency?
ghostQuestions.explanation: A totals 80 ms; B totals 30 ms. Fewer hops do not necessarily mean less delay.

ghostQuestions.prompt: A 5 ms route contains an unavailable link. A 20 ms route is fully available. Which can deliver under this model?
ghostQuestions.explanation: A failed link makes that route unavailable. Compare latency only among viable routes.

ghostQuestions.prompt: Two available routes total 10 + 10 ms and 5 + 15 ms. The objective is minimum latency. Which is acceptable?
ghostQuestions.explanation: Both total 20 ms, so both tied minimum-latency routes are accepted.

levels.title: Read the filter
levels.learningOutcome: Apply the first matching rule in an ordered packet filter.
levels.briefing: This small teaching filter checks rules from top to bottom and applies the first match. That ordering is the level's declared model, not a universal firewall configuration. A one-crossing edit temporarily allows the selected rule, then resets.

hints.method: Read each packet's protocol and destination port, then scan the ordered rules from the top until the first match.
hints.solution: The web request matches allow-web and passes. The admin request matches deny-admin and is dropped; the one-crossing edit can temporarily allow that rule.

completion.required: Pass a packet allowed by the active first-match policy.

checkpoints.title: Read the filter
checkpoints.briefing: This small teaching filter checks rules from top to bottom and applies the first match. That ordering is the level's declared model, not a universal firewall configuration. A one-crossing edit temporarily allows the selected rule, then resets.

hints.method: Read each packet's protocol and destination port, then scan the ordered rules from the top until the first match.
hints.solution: The web request matches allow-web and passes. The admin request matches deny-admin and is dropped; the one-crossing edit can temporarily allow that rule.

checkpoints.title: An earlier source exception
checkpoints.briefing: The first rule blocks a flagged source even though a later rule permits HTTPS. Choose a permitted packet, or deliberately arm the one-crossing exception.

hints.method: Check source address as well as protocol and port. Stop at the first matching rule.
hints.solution: Trusted-source HTTPS passes allow-web. Flagged-source HTTPS is denied by the earlier source rule unless its one-crossing edit is armed.

checkpoints.title: When no rule matches
checkpoints.briefing: This checkpoint deliberately uses default allow, unlike the earlier filters. It explicitly blocks DNS datagrams; unmatched telemetry follows the declared default.

hints.method: If no rule matches, read this checkpoint's default rather than assuming deny.
hints.solution: Telemetry matches no rule and passes by default allow. DNS matches deny-dns unless you apply its one-crossing edit.

ghostQuestions.prompt: The first rule denies TCP port 22. A later rule allows all TCP. What happens to a TCP packet for port 22?

choices.label: The first matching deny rule wins

ghostQuestions.explanation: The ordered first-match policy stops at the port-22 deny rule; it does not continue to a later allow.

ghostQuestions.prompt: No filter rule matches this packet, and the declared default is deny. What happens?
ghostQuestions.explanation: When no rule matches, the declared default action applies. This filter's default is deny.

ghostQuestions.prompt: You used a one-crossing edit to allow a normally denied packet. What policy applies to the next crossing?

choices.label: The edit stays active for the whole lesson

ghostQuestions.explanation: The temporary edit applies to one crossing only. The original filter rule applies afterward.

levels.title: Choose a transport
levels.learningOutcome: Choose transport behavior that fits an application's delivery need.
levels.briefing: TCP offers an ordered byte stream with retransmission behavior. UDP sends independent datagrams without transport-level delivery or retransmission guarantees; an application can add recovery. This level compares behavior, not movement speed.

challenge.need: A complete, ordered configuration file must arrive intact.
challenge.explanation: this task needs an ordered stream and transport retransmission behavior.

hints.method: Ask whether the application needs a reliable ordered stream or can handle independent datagrams itself.
hints.solution: Choose TCP for the complete ordered configuration file. UDP does not itself guarantee delivery or retransmission.

completion.required: Choose the transport behavior that fits the stated delivery need.

checkpoints.title: Choose a transport
checkpoints.briefing: TCP offers an ordered byte stream with retransmission behavior. UDP sends independent datagrams without transport-level delivery or retransmission guarantees; an application can add recovery. This level compares behavior, not movement speed.

hints.method: Ask whether the application needs a reliable ordered stream or can handle independent datagrams itself.
hints.solution: Choose TCP for the complete ordered configuration file. UDP does not itself guarantee delivery or retransmission.

checkpoints.title: Independent position updates
checkpoints.briefing: The application needs separate datagrams, handles missing updates itself, and explicitly does not want an ordered byte stream or transport retransmissions.

challenge.need: Send independent position-update datagrams; application code handles recovery and does not require transport ordering.
challenge.explanation: UDP preserves datagram boundaries without transport-level delivery, ordering, or retransmission guarantees; this application handles recovery itself.

hints.method: Match the requested message semantics, not a blanket claim about speed.
hints.solution: Choose UDP for these independent datagrams. Application recovery does not turn UDP itself into a reliable transport.

checkpoints.title: An ordered audit stream
checkpoints.briefing: A new task needs every log entry in order. Choose again for this need rather than repeating the last transport.

challenge.need: Transfer a complete audit log as an ordered byte stream with transport retransmission.
challenge.explanation: TCP provides an ordered byte stream with retransmission behavior; the application still defines log-record boundaries.

hints.method: Identify whether completeness and stream ordering are required.
hints.solution: Choose TCP. The application must frame its records within TCP's byte stream.

ghostQuestions.prompt: An application needs a complete, ordered byte stream with transport retransmission. Which transport matches?
ghostQuestions.explanation: TCP provides reliable, ordered byte-stream delivery with retransmission behavior. UDP itself does not.

ghostQuestions.prompt: A UDP datagram is lost. Which statement about UDP itself is correct?

choices.label: UDP has no delivery/retransmission guarantee; the application may add recovery

ghostQuestions.explanation: Recovery can be implemented above UDP, but it is not a transport-level guarantee provided by UDP.

ghostQuestions.prompt: An application sends several records over TCP. Who must define the record boundaries?

choices.label: The application, using framing within the byte stream
TCP automatically preserves each application's record

ghostQuestions.explanation: TCP delivers an ordered byte stream, not application message boundaries. The application supplies framing.

levels.title: Find the next hop
levels.learningOutcome: Use a prefix to decide whether a destination is local or needs a gateway.
levels.briefing: Compare the destination with the shown IPv4 prefix. A destination inside the local prefix is reached locally; an off-subnet destination is sent to the configured gateway. This lesson models one host and one configured prefix.

hints.method: Compare the destination's leading 24 bits with 192.0.2.0/24; only matching addresses are local.
hints.solution: 198.51.100.24 is outside 192.0.2.0/24, so send it to the configured gateway 192.0.2.1. The example 192.0.2.42 is local.

completion.required: Select local delivery or the configured gateway based on the prefix.

checkpoints.title: Find the next hop
checkpoints.briefing: Compare the destination with the shown IPv4 prefix. A destination inside the local prefix is reached locally; an off-subnet destination is sent to the configured gateway. This lesson models one host and one configured prefix.

hints.method: Compare the destination's leading 24 bits with 192.0.2.0/24; only matching addresses are local.
hints.solution: 198.51.100.24 is outside 192.0.2.0/24, so send it to the configured gateway 192.0.2.1. The example 192.0.2.42 is local.

checkpoints.title: A smaller local network
checkpoints.briefing: The local network is now 192.0.2.0/26, covering addresses 192.0.2.0 through 192.0.2.63. Compare the actual destination with that range.

hints.method: A /26 has blocks of 64 addresses. Use the prefix, not just the first three octets.
hints.solution: 192.0.2.62 is inside 192.0.2.0/26, so deliver locally.

checkpoints.title: Across the prefix boundary
checkpoints.briefing: The destination changes to 192.0.2.65 while the local prefix remains /26. The first three octets alone are not enough to decide.

hints.method: The local /26 stops at .63; .64 begins the next block.
hints.solution: 192.0.2.65 is outside 192.0.2.0/26. Send it to the configured gateway 192.0.2.1.

ghostQuestions.prompt: The local prefix is 192.0.2.0/24. Is destination 192.0.2.99 local or reached through the configured gateway?
ghostQuestions.explanation: 192.0.2.99 is inside 192.0.2.0/24, so this model delivers it locally.

ghostQuestions.prompt: The local prefix 192.0.2.0/26 covers .0 through .63. Where should a packet for 192.0.2.70 go?
ghostQuestions.explanation: The destination .70 lies outside the local /26 even though its first three octets match.

ghostQuestions.prompt: A host is on 192.0.2.64/26, covering .64 through .127. Is 192.0.2.90 inside this local prefix?
ghostQuestions.explanation: The address .90 is within the .64 through .127 block, so it is local to 192.0.2.64/26.

levels.title: Share the bottleneck
levels.learningOutcome: Apply a declared service order to traffic sharing a bottleneck.
levels.briefing: The shared link uses a strict-priority teaching queue: voice is served before bulk traffic when both are waiting. This is a local game policy, not a promise that priority traffic is immune to loss or failure.

hints.method: Check the declared queue policy and compare the classes waiting on the same link.
hints.solution: Voice is first in the stated strict-priority service order, ahead of bulk traffic.

completion.required: Choose the class with first service under the declared policy.

checkpoints.title: Share the bottleneck
checkpoints.briefing: The shared link uses a strict-priority teaching queue: voice is served before bulk traffic when both are waiting. This is a local game policy, not a promise that priority traffic is immune to loss or failure.

hints.method: Check the declared queue policy and compare the classes waiting on the same link.
hints.solution: Voice is first in the stated strict-priority service order, ahead of bulk traffic.

checkpoints.title: A control-traffic queue
checkpoints.briefing: This router declares a different strict-priority order: control traffic, then voice, then bulk. All three classes are waiting.

challenge.queuePolicy: strict priority: control before voice before bulk

hints.method: Read this router's configured priority order rather than assuming voice is always first.
hints.solution: Control traffic receives first service under this checkpoint's declared policy.

checkpoints.title: A reserved bulk-service slot
checkpoints.briefing: This teaching scheduler has reserved the current service slot for bulk transfer. Its displayed order applies to this round, not all future rounds.

challenge.queuePolicy: reserved bulk slot in the current service round

hints.method: Scheduling is a local policy. Which class owns the current slot?
hints.solution: Bulk receives first service in this reserved round. This does not imply immunity to packet loss.

ghostQuestions.prompt: A router declares service order control, voice, then bulk, and all three are waiting. Which is served first?

choices.label: Control, according to this router's policy

ghostQuestions.explanation: Service follows the declared local policy. Here control precedes voice and bulk.

ghostQuestions.prompt: Voice traffic has the highest queue priority. Does this guarantee that its packets cannot be lost?

choices.label: Yes, priority makes packets immune to loss
No, priority service is not a loss-free delivery guarantee

ghostQuestions.explanation: Queue priority determines service treatment; it does not eliminate link failures or every possible loss event.

ghostQuestions.prompt: The current scheduler round reserves its first service slot for bulk traffic. Which waiting class gets that slot?

choices.label: Bulk, under the declared current-round policy
Voice, regardless of the declared policy

ghostQuestions.explanation: The reserved bulk slot applies to this round. Other routers or later rounds may use a different service order.

levels.title: Manage delivery risk
levels.learningOutcome: Choose the lowest-risk route and distinguish route risk from a single delivery event.
levels.briefing: Risk points are a game model, not probabilities. Choose the lowest-risk route, optionally apply the four-point shielding action, then deliver. A scripted loss does not make a correct risk choice wrong; retry uses the next deterministic trace with no penalty.

linkEffects.explanation: Scripted queue overflow at the shared link.
The next scripted attempt is delivered.

hints.method: Add the risk points along each available route. The shielding action subtracts four points from the selected route, but the result is still a modeled score.
hints.solution: The lower route has the lowest risk after shielding. A first-trace drop is an environmental event; retry and the next authored trace delivers.

completion.required: Choose the lowest-risk strategy and successfully deliver the packet.

checkpoints.title: Manage delivery risk
checkpoints.briefing: Risk points are a game model, not probabilities. Choose the lowest-risk route, optionally apply the four-point shielding action, then deliver. A scripted loss does not make a correct risk choice wrong; retry uses the next deterministic trace with no penalty.

hints.method: Add the risk points along each available route. The shielding action subtracts four points from the selected route, but the result is still a modeled score.
hints.solution: The lower route has the lowest risk after shielding. A first-trace drop is an environmental event; retry and the next authored trace delivers.

checkpoints.title: Risk moves to another corridor
checkpoints.briefing: Recalculate the new risk scores. Shielding now removes two points. The route that was safest before need not be safest here.

hints.method: Sum each route's current risk and subtract the current shielding value.
hints.solution: Upper totals 3 risk points, or 1 with shielding; lower totals 6, or 4 shielded. Choose upper with shielding.

checkpoints.title: The final delivery window
checkpoints.briefing: The final segment has new risks and one-point shielding. After choosing, deliver through the exit; a scripted loss still permits a no-penalty retry.

hints.method: Use these final-segment risk values, not earlier checkpoints' scores.
hints.solution: Lower totals 3 risk points, or 2 with shielding. Choose lower with shielding, then retry if the first authored delivery trace drops.

ghostQuestions.prompt: Route A has 8 modeled risk points; route B has 4. A shield subtracts 1 point from either route. Which shielded route has lower risk?
ghostQuestions.explanation: The shielded scores are 7 and 3. B remains lower risk; this score does not guarantee delivery.

ghostQuestions.prompt: You chose the lowest-risk strategy, but one scripted delivery attempt dropped. Was the original strategy necessarily wrong?

choices.label: Yes, any drop proves the choice was wrong
No, keep the correct strategy and retry delivery

ghostQuestions.explanation: A single delivery event is separate from strategy grading. A correct risk choice is retained through the no-penalty retry.

ghostQuestions.prompt: A route has 6 risk points in this game. What does that mean?

choices.label: Exactly a 6 percent chance of packet loss
An authored comparison score, not a probability

ghostQuestions.explanation: Risk points compare the game's authored strategies. They are not measured loss probabilities.
